Aalborg is a North Sea port city in Denmark, located on Jutland Peninsula's north-eastern coast. By population (around 112,000) it is ranked the country's 4th largest - after Copenhagen, Aarhus and Odense. By road, the city is approx 65 km (40 mi) southwest of Frederikshavn, approx 120 km (73 mi) north of Aarhus and approx 410 km (255 mi) northwest of Copenhagen (Denmark's capital).

Port Aalborg handles over 60% of Denmark's shipping trade with Greenland. The port has 4 harbours - Marina Fjordparken (closest to downtown), Skudehavnen (used mainly by fishing boats and Sejlklubben Limfjorden / sailing club), Vestre Badehavn (adjacent to Skudehavnen / ~1 km from downtown) and Ostre Havn (Eastern Harbor, residential and commercial district, site of the former Aalborg Shipyard). Private ports are Aalborg Portland (serving the cement plant) and Vattenfall (serving the power station).

The town was established in the early-11th century, making it one of Denmark's oldest. Its strategic location (at Limfjorden's narrowest point) made it an important harbor port which later developed into a major industrial centre. The town is best-known for its half-timbered houses. Aalborg's current economy is based mainly on export shipping (grain, cement, coal, feedstuffs, fertilizers, spirits, oil cargoes), green-energy sectors (including production of rotors for wind turbines), information technologies, health support systems. City's largest companies and employers are Siemens Wind Power (turbine rotors), Aalborg Industries (manufacturer of marine boilers, burners, heat exchangers, inert gas systems), Aalborg Portland (cement producer), Telenor Denmark (telecommunications), Danisco (Danish Distillers, owned by Arcus ASA / Norway's largest wholesaler of wine and liquor).

Tourism is another fast-growing industry, with an increasing number of overnight tourists. The city is served by Aalborg Airport (civilian/military) located in Norresundby, approx 7 km (4 mi) northwest of Aalborg. The airport serves domestic and international flights linking to Amsterdam, UK (London), Norway (Oslo), Spain (Barcelona, Malaga). Seasonal flights connect to Turkey (Antalya), Greece (Crete, Cyprus), Spain (Mallorca, Gran Canaria), Faroe Islands (Vagar), Sweden (Bornholm).

Among city's most popular landmarks are Budolfi Catedral (15th-century), Aalborg Kloster (15th-century monastery), Alborghus Slot (16th-century castle), Aalborg Historiske Museum (with Viking relics), marine museum, military museum, Kunsten Museum (modern art), zoo, large nature parks, Tivoliland (theme park).

2019 was Aalborg cruise port's record season with handled 35 ship calls and ~30,000 tourists. For 2020 were projected min 45 ship calls and ~36,000 tourists.

Aalborg cruise terminal

In July 2019, Port Aalborg introduced a new policy that limits the number of daily visiting cruise ships (calls) to one per day. The new rule was prompted by the increasing number of cruise vessels and their passengers-crew to Denmark's only inland cruise port. In the period 2014-2018, cruiser numbers increased from ~1000 (2014) to ~40,000 (2018). For 2019 were scheduled 34 ship calls and for 2020 were booked 45.

In 2019, Aalborg's Royal Cruise Berth was deepened/dredged to allow docking of vessels with max LOA length 255 m (837 ft).

Aalborg is one of the easier Danish cruise ports to explore independently. Most cruise calls use Honnørkajen, the Royal Cruise Berth directly on the city waterfront beside Aalborghus Castle. From here, the historic center, pedestrian streets and main waterfront sights are only a few minutes away on foot.

At a Glance

  • Independent sightseeing: Easy independently for ships at Honnørkajen.
  • Arrival: Ships normally dock rather than tender.
  • Main berth: Honnørkajen/Royal Cruise Berth in central Aalborg.
  • Walking: The old town begins about 0.3-0.6 km (0.2-0.4 mi) from the berth.
  • Terrain: Mostly flat, with some cobblestones and uneven paving in older streets.
  • Best use of a short call: Historic center and waterfront on foot.
  • For a longer call: Add Lindholm Høje Viking site or Kunsten Museum of Modern Art.

Getting from the Cruise Port

Honnørkajen is directly in front of Aalborghus Castle and forms part of Aalborg's public waterfront. Passengers can normally start sightseeing immediately after leaving the ship. Nytorv, Østerågade and the pedestrian shopping streets are around a 5-10 minute walk away, while the Utzon Center is also only a few minutes from the berth.

Not every ship necessarily uses Honnørkajen. The Port of Aalborg's current cruise schedule occasionally assigns vessels to Berth 4110, a commercial quay roughly 2 km (1.2 mi) from the central sightseeing area. If your ship uses an alternative berth, follow the onboard instructions for the passenger exit and any shuttle or transfer arrangements rather than assuming that the city-center walking route applies.

Taxis are most useful for attractions outside the center. Aalborg also has a local bus network, with several routes serving central stops such as Nytorv and Vesterbro.

Best Ways to Spend Your Time

Historic Aalborg and the Waterfront

Allow: 2-3 hours. Transport: Walk. Independent sightseeing: Very easy.

This is the most practical choice for a first visit. From the ship, combine Aalborghus Castle, Jens Bang's Renaissance house, Budolfi Cathedral and the small historic streets around Hjelmerstald with the modern Limfjord waterfront. The Utzon Center and Musikkens Hus provide a strong contrast to the older city and are still within easy walking distance of the ship.

Lindholm Høje Viking Site and Museum

Allow: about 2.5-3.5 hours. Distance: approximately 4.5 km (2.8 mi) from central Aalborg. Independent sightseeing: Practical with some planning.

Lindholm Høje, across the Limfjord in Nørresundby, combines a large Iron Age and Viking burial ground with a museum explaining the site and Viking life around the fjord. A taxi generally takes around 10-15 minutes. Public buses from central Aalborg can also reach the Lindholm Høje area in roughly 15-20 minutes, but check the current timetable before leaving the city center.

The outdoor archaeological site is on a hill and includes grass and uneven ground. Visitors with limited mobility may find the museum easier than the burial field itself.

Kunsten Museum of Modern Art

Allow: about 2-3 hours including transport. Distance: roughly 2 km (1.2 mi) from Honnørkajen. Independent sightseeing: Easy.

Kunsten is particularly worthwhile for passengers interested in modern art and Scandinavian architecture. The building was designed by Alvar Aalto, Elissa Aalto and Jean-Jacques Baruël. It can be reached in around 25-30 minutes on foot from the waterfront or more quickly by taxi or local transport. Check the museum's opening hours for the day of your call before making it the main part of your visit.

Rebild Bakker and Rold Skov

Allow: at least 4-5 hours. Distance: about 30 km (18.6 mi) south of Aalborg. Independent sightseeing: Possible by car; organized excursion recommended for most cruise visitors.

The heath-covered hills of Rebild Bakker and the neighboring Rold Skov forest are around a 30-minute drive from Aalborg. They suit passengers wanting countryside rather than city sightseeing, but public-transport connections consume considerably more port time. A ship excursion, private tour or pre-arranged taxi is more practical when the call is short.

Self-Guided Walking Tour

Old Town and Waterfront Loop

Start: Honnørkajen/Royal Cruise Berth. Distance: approximately 3 km (1.9 mi). Pure walking time: about 40-45 minutes. Recommended total time: 2-3 hours. Difficulty: Easy, with some cobbled streets.

  1. Aalborghus Castle: Begin immediately beside the cruise berth. Walk through the grounds and view the half-timbered castle buildings.
  2. Nytorv and Jens Bang's House: Walk into the historic center to see one of Aalborg's best-known Renaissance buildings on Østerågade.
  3. Budolfi Cathedral and Gammeltorv: Continue through the pedestrian area to Aalborg's cathedral and the surrounding historic square.
  4. Hjelmerstald: Detour into this small cobbled street of low historic houses. The paving here is less even than the main pedestrian streets.
  5. Utzon Center: Return toward the Limfjord and follow the waterfront to Jørn Utzon's architecture and design center.
  6. Musikkens Hus: Continue east along the promenade to Aalborg's modern concert hall and cultural waterfront.
  7. Return to Honnørkajen: Retrace the waterfront promenade west to the ship.

The route is largely flat and keeps you close to the ship throughout most of the day. It can easily be shortened by turning back at the Utzon Center or extended with cafés, shopping streets or an indoor museum visit.

Practical Tips

Aalborg's center is compact enough that there is little reason to book an organized city tour unless you prefer a guide. Excursions become more useful for Lindholm Høje combined with other sights, or for countryside destinations such as Rebild Bakker and Rold Skov.

Denmark uses the Danish krone, and card/contactless payment is widely used. Weather beside the Limfjord can be windy and change quickly, so a light waterproof layer is useful even when the forecast is generally good.

For sightseeing entirely within central Aalborg, plan to return to the berth with at least 30-45 minutes in reserve before the ship's stated all-aboard time. If visiting Lindholm Høje or anywhere outside the city center, leave a larger margin for traffic, bus delays and the final transfer back to the correct berth.
